utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, you wanted to make some submissions. But perhaps before doing so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. You will remember that in yesterday's hearing there were certain points that I wished to raise before Mr. Ierace takes the floor, and you told me to speak at the end of yesterday's hearing. I can do this now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do it now, but try to do it in five minutes and not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will do it in five minutes, and not to waste any time, I would like to add another two points. The first thing that I wish to see is not a protest, something I wish to contest; it's just to establish facts with regard to the war in Algeria. We wish to ask questions on this subject with the witness of yesterday, who could have answered these questions in closed session. The Defence would like to say that its rights have been violated, and it is saying clearly that this has been the case for the record. These are not questions relating to issues of 40 years back, but we speak today of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, yesterday a decision has been taken on it. That's the end of the discussion. We're not going to debate on why its the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say it was a just or a false decision. The Defence simply considers that its rights have been violated, and I will stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I said that there's no room for debate at this moment on this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second point I wish to has to do with the witness Philips. We made an application yesterday. We will communicate it to you in the course of the day. We wish to add something orally. As regards Witness Philips, in regards to the witness Ewa Tabeau -- do I have time to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I won't have enough time. Five minutes will not be enough. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't want to use the five minutes, then please write down what you have to submit to the Court in addition to what you have written already. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you could, in some seven minutes, tell the Court...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have provided two documents which will assist me in keeping my submission brief. While they are being handed out, on the 8th of May, pursuant to the direction that the Prosecution finish its case by the 5th of July, I provided a fresh witness list which involved the deletion of some 63 witnesses, I think it was, from the Prosecution case, and I indicated that the Prosecution would additionally reduce significantly the anticipated time that the remaining witnesses would take in chief. I also said that there were two factors which were not reflected in that list. The first was a decision in relation to the 92 bis witnesses, and the second was the requirements by the Defence as to cross-examination time for expert witnesses. Mr. President, the 92 bis application was filed yesterday. It wasn't, in fact, until this week that we received the last of the translations. We have filed -- I'm sorry. We have filed 21 witness statements, so we have deleted 2. In addition, we have deleted from those 21 a number of the annexures and we have placed in a more accessible order for your convenience that material to make it easier to peruse. Mr. President, the Defence, pursuant to your requirement filed on Tuesday a document which set out a document which they require to cross-examine expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can announce to you and to the Defence that the time requested for cross-examination of the expert witnesses will not be granted to the number of hours indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be considerably reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, unfortunately, that will not overcome the problem which the Prosecution now faces. The pace of evidence has been significantly less than the Prosecution would have hoped for in spite of the Prosecution taking every possible measure to maintain it. Mr. President, I want it to be clearly understood that I am not in any way seeking to place blame on the Defence or the Trial Chamber or anyone else. That is simply not the issue. The issue is this: That the Prosecution, having done everything it possibly could, we simply cannot keep to a timetable which will enable us to complete the bare requirements of our case in order to fairly present the Prosecution case in a minimal sense and still finish by the 5th of July. I come to the document which comprises a number of charts. The first chart is one that I have prepared overnight. It analyses the time taken by nine of the witnesses that we have called since the 8th of May. There are four witnesses who have not been analysed, two because I did not have precise times available overnight, one because he's part heard, and another because his evidence was only finished yesterday. So in the third column, we have the 65 ter original estimate of evidence in chief, and I emphasise "in chief." Alongside we have the revised estimate. Alongside that, we have the total time by Prosecution, in other words, not just in chief, but also re-examination. And then alongside that, total time taken by the Defence, not just cross-examination, but any further cross-examination. And then in the last column, the time taken by questions from Your Honours. Mr. President, on the bottom row, we see some totals. Total 65 ter estimate does not include Eterovic because there was not a total for him, but nevertheless, 25 hours, leaving him out of it. Revised estimate, we are able to drop it to 19 and a half hours, but of course that included for the first time an estimate for Eterovic. In relation to the total time taken by the Prosecution, it is clear that we were well within the revised estimate, including re-examination, we came in at three quarters, roughly, of that revised estimate. Cross-examination, a little more than the time taken by the Defence, additional two hours, and then two hours for questions from the Bench. Mr. President, I've sought to add two additional factors. Firstly, I anticipate, as the Defence has done many times, that it will say that the Prosecution has unduly slowed down the pace of cross-examination by unnecessary objections, and rather than drag this Trial Chamber into a futile match of allegation and counter-allegation, I have cleaned up the transcript of two of the witnesses. In other words, I took the transcript and took out every intervention by the opposing party so we could see how much hard evidence there was. The two witnesses that I selected were Kolp. He was taken by Mr. Mundis, and Niaz, who was taken by me. So it allows for different styles from the Prosecution. The cleaned-up evidence appears, those times appear in brackets, and one can see in relation to Kolp what those figures are, how they compare, in other words, the Prosecution, instead of two hours, took one hour and 22 minutes, Defence took one hour and 52 minutes. In relation to Niaz, the Prosecution took one hour and 3 minutes and the Defence took one hour. But there's another factor, and that is that during examination-in-chief over the last few weeks, the Defence has repeatedly risen to its feet and complained about the quality of the French transcript, its accuracy. I do not for a minute, I repeat myself, seek to be critical of the Defence, of the French translators, or anyone else. What is simply relevant for this exercise is that it slows down the Prosecution, and it is a factor beyond the Prosecution's control. To give you an example of how often that happens, in relation to the evidence of Kolp, during that examination, the one hour and 29 minutes, there were 11 objections by the Defence, based simply -- I'm sorry, sixth of which were based simply on complaints about the French transcript. And if one goes to the evidence of Henneberry, during the examination-in-chief there were a total of 16 objections by the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, looking at the clock and looking at your piece of paper, I see that you're more or less reflecting what is on paper. Could you please proceed, because we will carefully read what you have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I leave it, can I make one more point about the chart? In relation to Niaz, if one looks at those cleaned-up times, one would expect there to be more hard evidence from the Prosecution than the Defence, one hour 3 minutes for the Prosecution, one hour for the Defence. In fact, when one cleans up that hard copy of transcript, it comes down to 14 pages for the Prosecution, 15 for the Defence. That reflects, that quantifies the difference pace between examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, even where the Prosecution and Defence have exactly the same period of time, the Defence can produce more evidence because they can speak faster, the witnesses can speak faster, and they can get through more questions and more answers. Good luck to the Defence, Mr. President. I'm not complaining about them. I'm simply making the point that in terms of us keeping to our timetable, these are the insurmountable problems we face. Mr. President, to go to the remaining charts, and before I do that, in conjunction, I refer you to the memo addressed to me dated the 4th of June from the chief of the VWU, following a meeting I had with her, in which she said, as she repeats in this memo, that they are at a point of effectively seizure. In our attempts to make sure that not five minutes of court time is wasted, so that we can meet the deadline, there have been a number of witnesses who have come to The Hague to give evidence who have become part heard or not reached, simply because we have not been able to keep to the timetable that we foreshadow seven days in advance. Put simply, the VWU cannot maintain this level of intensity, and that point has been made in clear terms to me. We have seen an example of that this week. We have Mr. Mole this morning. I am reliably informed that he is, to put it mildly, less than happy, and one can well imagine why. He gave some evidence on Monday, having arrived last weekend. He will give at best another hour's evidence today and then have to come back at some later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We do understand that this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a very unpleasant situation for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I come now to the chart. In constructing this chart, the Prosecution has sought to indicate to the Tribunal a more realistic timetable. I do not for a minute suggest that if we adopt this timetable that there will be a wasted five minutes. Rather, in applying this timetable, we do not have witnesses at great expense waiting in the wings, so as to speak. Mr. President, when one applies the remaining witness list to the forthcoming weeks and factors in the break, the Plenary Sessions, and so on, it becomes apparent that the Prosecution requires, until the 30th of August, in order to get through its viva voce witnesses, and that assumes that we are successful in relation to our 92 bis application. I appreciate, Mr. President, that you said this morning that the Defence will not receive the time that they have requested. Mr. President, in the remaining few minutes that are allocated to me, I appreciate I've gone beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid there are no more minutes allocated to you. May I take it that this is what you suggest that would be the order of witnesses to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Rough order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rough order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just say this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We are now in the -- I think we're at the 96th or 97th day of hearing. We've been going since December. Mr. President, I would like to think that the Prosecution has been viewed as doing everything it could throughout that period to meet the requirements of the Trial Chamber and in so doing that the Trial Chamber could have some degree of confidence that the Prosecution can be trusted to present its case in as efficient a manner as possible. And in making these submissions perhaps for the first time since December, I specify a date. That date, of course, and this timetable, again assumes that nothing goes wrong, that no time is lost, and that there is not a blowout, so as to speak, in terms of legal arguments and so on. So I simply make the point, Mr. President, that perhaps we're at a stage where the Prosecution can be -- the Trial Chamber can have a degree of confidence that if there is some latitude given to the Prosecution, that that latitude will not result in any less efficient a presentation of its case and that one could accept from the Prosecution that we are talking about the bare minimum in terms of an issue of fundamental fairness. The bare minimum that is required to allow the Prosecution to present its case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have an opportunity to respond, and we'd like to start with the next witness at 9.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. 0836, 0851, the Prosecution used up only 220 minutes of the time that you accorded it. This is perhaps one of the reasons that time is being lost. I don't blame anyone. I'm just taking note of the situation. What I wish to do is to make a suggestion, only one example. Yesterday we listened for a very long time, almost half an hour, an integral text of a telephone conversation for which only a few seconds would have been necessary. The Defence believes that this could be cut down. We would have been the first to cooperate with the Prosecution in that sense. We have to manage time better, and the Defence counsel is at the disposal of the Prosecution for this if it so desires. Just a few words by way of conclusion. You will have noted, as most anyone else, that the rare interventions of the Defence on technical matters are made only when it is necessary and not, as a rule, on questions of detail. It is our duty to verify the transcripts, and what I would suggest, to gain time - and we discussed this matter with the representatives of the French government, and this is what goes on at Rwanda - that we should pass directly to the French transcripts, and I think that the Chamber is bilingual, and in this way we would gain time in future, and the Prosecution will be completely satisfied. This is one of the ideas that I could put forward if the Prosecution agrees, and that we could perhaps decide on. As regards the Defence's interventions, they are necessary, and the figures that have been submitted to us, although they represent a lot of work, perhaps not useful and justified, do not really reflect the realities. The Defence is much briefer than the Prosecution, and if necessary, it intervenes in written, which the Prosecution could do at times also. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ierace, that you want the Chamber to decide on whether this time schedule would be acceptable for the Chamber. We'll try, if not to give a decision, at least give some guidance today. It's a complex matter, so therefore I cannot promise you that, as I told you yesterday, that we could decide in three hours on five weeks. But we'll see whether we can give you some guidance by the end of this morning's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there are three minutes left, three and a half minutes left. I don't know whether you want to use that time in order to make the submissions you couldn't do before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting. I simply wanted to correct something. I did indicate yesterday that it was five weeks. In fact, Mr. President, you will see it's six weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It makes it even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As regards - and I will keep to the time limit - as regards the Witness Philips, what we would like to add is that the situation is similar to the situation in the Milosevic case. We know that -- father's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any problem, please address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Means the people who are your equals, your Judges, were confronted with a situation, a similar situation, where expert witnesses were called, when in fact these were members of the Prosecution, of the OTP. I think that an oral decision has been made in that sense. As regards the two witnesses, at least in regard to Mr. Phillips, it is not a witness that was a witness to the facts, counted bodies in a ditch or witnessed a shelling. It was a witness who elaborated theories, who spoke of figures and submitted reports, and this is quite different to have a visual witness who said, "I saw this. I witnessed that" than a witness who elaborated a conception, a report. And I hope that I'm still within my time limit. And we oppose on the basis of those witnesses are -- but the Prosecution and nothing else, that they should be heard. [As interpreted] We oppose the production of such reports for the motives that we have set forth in our application that we wrote yesterday and which we will communicate to you today. This was simply what I wished to add. The other point I wish to raise is the programme of today. We do not know who will be heard in a while, Mr. President, but if it is Mr. Van Baal, we would like to say the following. Neither General Galic nor Ms. Pilipovic had the time to read and then to examine the document, so that even if it were only an examination-in-chief right now, no one here would be capable of listening, of hearing what is to be heard, for the simple fact that we did not have time to prepare, and therefore we're in a situation where we are not able to work, and we would like to point Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this out. And thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has taken notice of your objection against the examination of Philips and Tabeau as expert witnesses for the reasons you indicated. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would make sense, I think, for you and Your Honours to look at his material before we take that debate further, and that could happen after the week's break. It's simply a chart with a two-page statement, summarising hundreds and hundreds of documents. Mr. President, Witness AD, I've received the decision. The Defence has swore the certificate. I'd be grateful if that could be resolved so as to enable us to take the necessary steps either way. If, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber does contemplate issuing a certificate, I would seek to be heard on that. It would not take long. But if it was possible for a decision about the certificate to be made or communicated to the Prosecution, either today or during the course of next week, I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll let you know whether additional oral argument is of any use in regard of the certificate requested. If so, we'll let you know when it will take place; and if not, we'll also inform you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question mark is who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's Richard Mole. General Van Baal is expected to arrive at 11.00, so at whatever point he's brought to the door of the courtroom, then we will suspend Richard Mole and proceed with General Van Baal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, it seems to me that we have not yet decided regarding the evidence produced during Witness W.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're perfectly right. Thank you very much for assisting me. That's what happens when you start so early. We should have to do it in closed session, so therefore let us turn into closed session right now and ask the usher to wait one second with Mr. Mole. Could we turn into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to apologise for the very bad situation for you that you had to wait for quite some time. We are facing some major scheduling problems. I hope you'll understand, but I am and this Chamber is fully aware of the unpleasant situation that has been created by these problems. I hope you will accept this. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I still remind you you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P3704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the coloured map?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's the coloured map, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was distributed already, although I must admit that I don't have it with me at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, when you last gave evidence on Monday, I asked you whether you recollected any military offensives by the Romanija Corps, and you said, "One in particular that I recall was the offensive in the area of Otes, which was on the west side of Sarajevo during the early days of 1992." You were then shown this map, and you explained to us how this map came into being, in particular, the confrontation line which appears on it, or at least the line which appears on it. Is that the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that you placed that line on the map the date after the 10th of December, 1992. How were you able to determine that it was after that date?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict which had occurred in the Otes region in the period of early December caused the adjustment to the front line map to exclude Otes from the area of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the Otes campaign?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The early part of December, leading up to the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please place that part of the map which shows Otes under the screen in such a way with the usher's help, so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an objection to the term "campaign," for legal and technical reasons. I do not think that Otes was a campaign as such, as perhaps as some other campaigns that we know, the campaign in Russia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To save time, Mr. President, I'll change the terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We will refer to it as the Otes offensive?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think we're having some trouble getting the map onto the computer screens, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just have the -- well, we don't see anything apart that there is something under the ELMO. Could you please put it as flat as possible, Madam Usher, or zoom it in in such a way, because it might be... I think it should be more flat and then perhaps adjust it to... No, it doesn't seem to be that part, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll avoid the use of the ELMO at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see now -- there we were. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we can zoom in a little. All right. Stopping there for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, can you point to the area of Otes on the map and hold your finger or the pointer at that place so that the camera can adjust to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If we could zoom yes. Yes. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So I think your evidence is that the offensive by the Romanija Corps was successful in that they captured the area of Otes, thus changing the position of the confrontation line in that part of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please take a blue marker. At that stage, whereabouts, in what building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a blue marker, just to be sure? It's not a black marker? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the UN headquarters, your headquarters included? What was the name of the building?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building was the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please place a cross where that building was, just a little blue cross.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And if you could just write "PTT" alongside it, as small as you can.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, did you see any of the fighting that took place in the Otes offensive?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see whether any artillery and mortars and tanks were deployed by the Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but not from the PTT building. We were from another observation point. It was called Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us your assessment of the degree of use of artillery and mortars by the Romanija Corps during that battle?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until that time, it was the most intense shelling that we had experienced, certainly in Sarajevo. We estimated the number of rounds that impacted the area of concern to be about 1.500, but there were parameters which I must explain. The hours of daylight were limited. There was fog in the region. And so our observation time was limited. So one could probably assess that the numbers of rounds would be double within a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that stage were the Lima observation posts operating?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And what reports, if any, were you receiving as to the activity of the various artillery batteries during that period on the Lima side, in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those that we were monitoring were extremely busy, without going far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And did you draw any conclusions or make any observations based on what you saw of the use of artillery in particular by the Romanija Corps in that offensive as to the degree of control and coordination of the Romanija Corps and its leadership?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and control of the artillery positions was such that they could bring to bear a very effective fire mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That map could be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your dealings with General Galic, did you ever have cause to call on him to assist you with any problems involving relationships between your subordinate UNMOs and his forces?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever call on him to take any action in relation to that issue or those issues?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at least two events which involved UNMOs being held illegally by individuals on the Serb side. For different reasons. If I may give one example. One of the individuals and their family, who kept the UNMOs restrained, was extremely upset at the loss of a relative, and it was their method of bringing that to people's attention. So that would be an example of our UNMOs being kept in inappropriate circumstances. I asked General Galic to assist, either directly or through the headquarters on the Lima side, and that assistance was given effectively, efficiently, and quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMOs were released and returned to duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether any disciplinary action was taken against his forces who were involved in either of those incidents that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that it was the equivalent of military police, who were involved under his orders, but I don't know any further than that as to what happened to the individuals concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is it that you recollect that leads you to say that you presume that military police were involved? What do you know of? What do you recollect specifically as to disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was what I was told from my officers on the Lima side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that the military police had been involved in the release of the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, merely to gain time. I do not have the impression that this line of examination is all that relevant. It would be unnecessary and I am therefore objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there's a question, you think it's irrelevant, you may object against that question, not against a line of questioning in general. But what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, then we'll say that the questioned is asked to know whether in this case when the military police supposedly intervened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That was not the question. That was the answer, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, could you please briefly explain the relevance of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This evidence demonstrates the ability of the accused at that particular period, that is, late 1992, to exert control over his subordinates. Here we have an incident where his forces had taken certain action against some UNMOs, and when he so desired, he was able to issue orders and take steps to intervene forcefully to bring about his desired result. So that's the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to thank General Galic following one of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever he assisted me, and in these particular instances, I did thank him, either directly when I next saw him or through my officers on Lima side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit -- I think it is 3708.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that letter in front of you?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might do eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on from that. I don't think we need the letter. It may be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think we have a 3708, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On occasions that you visited -- I withdraw that. Do you recall when it was, approximately, that those incidents took place, that is, where General Galic intervened?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates, no doubt, would be in my original statement, but I don't recall the dates set here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall the months, or approximately the months?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm struggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. On the occasions that you visited Lukavica, did you ever go to the operations room?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And we're talking, of course, about the operations room of the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw in terms of its layout, visual aids, communications, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was laid out in the conventional fashion for an operations room, with maps, telephones, radios, duty officer, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have any particular expertise in the area of logistics?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my -- or was my main task, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when you say that was your main task, was that before or after you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been serving in the military for 24 years, and in most of that period had served in the Royal Corps Transport, a logistic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us just a little bit about what's involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the French interpretation. I believe this witness spoke in the past tense, and in the French interpretation I see that interpreters are indicating with their heads -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us just briefly what's involved in logistics in relation to a military campaign?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provision of all items required in that campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when you say "all items," does that include munitions? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that you -- I withdraw that. Did you travel to the Lima side on a regular basis or an irregular basis?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. How often would you visit the observation posts on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would visit probably three, four times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that one of the objectives i setting up the -- in positioning the Lima OPs was to maximize the opportunity of observing artillery and heavy weapons. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Firstly, when you toured the Lima observation posts, I take it that you saw the heavy weaponry that was near those posts?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see any munitions in those areas?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the -- what type of munitions would you see at those sites?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be the heavy rounds associated with the weapons on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What steps, if any, were taken to protect the munitions from incoming artillery, mortars, and the like, typically?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the common features of all the Lima sites was that the weapons were in the open, the ammunition was in the open. None of both of those items were camouflaged. The soldiers and officers that manned them sometimes were in uniform, sometimes not, being in civilian clothes, and the whole atmosphere of the weapon sites was relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the fact that the shells were in the open tell you anything, in terms of your expertise and military experience, as to the degree of perceived threat by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The threat perceived by themselves was low, very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell us something as to the quantities of shells that you saw at these sites?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can use my own military experience to explain how I would interpret that, would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our military, as a planning guide, we use an expression called the daily ammunition expenditure rate, which here is best abbreviated to DAER. It is a planning guide that we, as logisticians utilise to plan how many rounds for each weapon, for the unit that we are supplying, is provided on a daily basis for normal use. Clearly, if the usage increases, so does the DAER for different phases of battle. Using that as a basis of the ammunition that we saw on the weapon sites, my estimate would be that they had probably between one and two DAERs available to them on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And how would that rate in terms -- in a general sense, in terms of whether that is a little, average, or a lot?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, as a DAER, would be an average.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations that would suggest that the heavy weaponry on the Romanija Corps site was poorly supplied with munitions?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never an occasion when we considered that it was poorly resupplied. They generally seemed to have as much ammunition as they required. We often saw the resupply runs. They were unhindered. So no, there was no reason to believe that they would be short of munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going back briefly to the DAER, is it possible for you to give us an idea of what number of shells would be required for a particular type of weapon, say a particular type of Howitzer or field gun?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the use of this terminology would be British, it's difficult to transpose that across to a different military. But to best answer your question, on a weapon site of, for example, a battery, a field battery, one would expect to see a stockpile of five, six hundred rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And for how many guns would that be?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: A battery, which would be --?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Again in terms of logistics, as you understand it, would a commander typically require detailed information as to the use of munitions, that is, the rate of use of munitions?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any commander would have an artillery representative who would advise him of all matters relating to his arm. Crucial to that would be resupply, and if any problem to that resupply had occurred, it would be the duty of the artillery commander to bring it to the attention of the commander, because clearly it would be a limiting factor to the commander's capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the case of the Romanija Corps, in a general sense, in terms of its assets, what was its principal weakness - and I include human assets - and what was its principal strength, at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disposition of both the forces, either side, was opposites in that the Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but in the French interpretation there was a contradiction which is possibly due, in line 20... I do not know if a word was interpreted correctly. Thank you. Sorry for this interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate what word?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Weakness. It was said which was the chief -- the principal force, whereas the sense of the original was exactly the contrary. But it has now been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I give you some guidance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If this would have occurred, you could have said, "As far as I know, the word weakness in line 20 seems not to have been translated, or not correctly translated." That would be just enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will say it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The disposition of either side in the conflict was such that they were opposite, and I illustrate that by explaining that the Romanija Corps was heavy on artillery and heavy weapons, but very light, or comparatively light, on infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I'll stop you there, in the interests of saving time. It being the case that one would presumably expect the commander of the Romanija Corps to depend on his artillery as his principal strength; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To what extent would that, in your opinion, impact on his need to maintain a close monitoring of the use of his artillery?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You'll just have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will rephrase that. I apologise for that. Given his dependency on artillery, that being his principal strength, would you expect the commander to carefully monitor the use of it?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would that extend to both the rate of use of the munitions and the type of target or not?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a logical progression from what we're discussing in that if there is an ammunition expenditure on a daily basis, which there was, it had to be recorded and be known. If, therefore, ammunition was being replaced on a daily basis, it must be going somewhere. So the question begs: Where was it going? As a commander, I would hope to know where it was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the batteries being resupplied?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What sort of vehicles were involved in that? If you could tell us what typically you would see.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were never the very large resupply vehicles, say, of 10 tonnes. They tended to be the smaller vehicles, up to about five tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going back momentarily to Otes, you've told us that at that stage that was the heaviest frequency of recorded fire, and even that was in the context of limited viewing hours. During that offensive, can you give us a range of incoming impacts from the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb army side into Sarajevo? In other words, over the days of the offensive, what type of number of rounds are we talking about coming in?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned before, the estimate on a daily basis was 1.500 seen, therefore probably double that in any 24-hour period, and that multiplied by a function of six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware as to where the munitions came from that were used by the Romanija Corps? And in particular, I'm talking about heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, all the weapon sites were clearly very busy, both for the fire missions that they were on, and obviously being resupplied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the vicinity in Serb-held territory there were any munitions factories?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's one that I know of, yes, Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long was the front line around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: We estimated it at 64, 65 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever circumnavigate the city on the Serb side whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I take it that was driving?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Myself and two others took a jeep and went right around the front line on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long did it take you?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very long day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given that you were able to do that, you being a military observer, are you aware of any impediment that would have confronted the commander of the Romanija Corps had he wished to visit any part of the front line during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disposition of the front line meant that physical travel from one side to the other was of necessity going to take a long time. The roads were very narrow, the terrain was very hilly, and therefore overall progress was slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But are you aware of any impediment to him doing it, had he wished to do it?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going back to the ability of the leadership of the Romanija Corps to intervene when they wished, was there any incident in which you were a participant where intervention from a higher level was called upon?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you indicate what level that might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps I'll do it a different way. Were you ever involved in an incident where you called upon your contacts with higher leadership within the Romanija Corps to assist to extricate you from a different situation?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may give an example of one of our functions was the arrangement of body swaps between sides. This required immense amount of planning, and to achieve that I had meetings on the airport with representatives of both sides. I used to collect the representatives from the Presidency side because I lived in the city, and take them to the airport. The incident to which I refer, myself and the Presidency representatives were taken in two French APCs back towards the city from the airport. At the checkpoint on the airport road by Nedzarici, a T54 tank and APC on the Serb side prevented further progress. The situation became extremely tense in that they wished to open the APC rear doors, which eventually was done. I was in the company of an RCMP sergeant, Hull, and myself, were in the back seats, nearest the door, when they were opened. The Serb soldiers were intent on removing the Presidency representatives to execute them. We had -- we, Sergeant Hull and myself, intended obviously to prevent that, and for 20 minutes we worked very hard, amidst jostling, to prevent that event occurring. I then asked, when the situated permitted, that I could speak to their commander, and I mentioned him by name, although I don't recall the name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt for a minute. Did you in fact make a decision, that is, you and Officer Hull, between yourselves that come what may you would not move?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the decision we had come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I named their commander by name, there was a certain degree of restraint, and after maybe an hour and a half, the individual who I had asked for arrived on the scene. By good fortune, I had had lunch with this individual that day, and the situation was quickly resolved and we were able to proceed on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that the commander arrived, the situation resolved, and you were on your way. What was the connection? In other words, once the commander arrived, did he say anything? Did he give any orders?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I not only had had lunch that day, but there had been on one occasion an observation point on the Papa side -- no. I withdraw that - close to the Papa side, right in Nedzarici, within the command area of the Serb commander would we're referring to. So I knew him from that as well, not just lunch. It was not a social visit. Because of that connection, he was able then to command his soldiers to effect our continued journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, do I understand you to be saying - please correct me if I'm wrong - that he was a commander from the area of Nedzarici, in other words, that was his area of command?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his name?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the period -- before I move on: Do you recollect the approximate date of that incident?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if we look in my original witness statement, the date is included within.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We'll come to some reports later. During the period that you were in Sarajevo, can you give us some idea of the daily frequency of sniper fire, mortar impacts, shell impacts inside the city throughout the 24-hour period? If I could first of all ask you this: Was there a day that you recollect where there were no shell impacts in the city?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely in the. May I not. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was continual background noise of small arms and mortars and artillery throughout all the time that I spent in Sarajevo from September to December 1992. It was a constant background, something it takes a lot to get used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please try not to be too cryptic. What do you mean by "it takes a lot to get used to"? I think you should spell that out.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, one has to assess what you perceive as normal, and very quickly, when living in the city, one learnt that normal was this persistent, constant level of tension created by small arms, mortars, and heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to the comparative levels of damage as a result of incoming shell fire to military areas as opposed to civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, let me define my understanding of the distinction between the two. Clearly, any activity around front lines, any activity around known headquarters, any activity around logistics elements, I would consider military targets. The remainder definitely wasn't. I knew where those military targets were. It would be unbelievable that anybody else who was targeting those areas didn't know where they were, which left large sways of the city, in my opinion, to be not areas of a target, military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having explained that, how did the damage compare between the two types of areas?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you mean physical damage to buildings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, the damage around the front lines was extensive, because those front lines seldom moved, as perhaps I've begun to explain. The map we've already seen had a front line on it which changed little, except for the Otes area, in four months. So clearly the front lines were a very damaged area of the city. However, the remainder of the city showed immense damage from incoming munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Leaving aside the signs of physical damage from past activity, and focusing instead on your observations of incoming fire, how did that compare, while you were there, that is, incoming fire in the areas of military targets, as you have defined them, and areas which you regarded as non-military-target areas?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, in the time I was there, there were moments, numerous moments, that the front line was extremely active, but the background noise and overall pressure upon the city was a constant. The only thing that varied in that regard was the intensity, for example, of shelling and mortaring, within the city generally. It went up and it went down, sometimes connected to perceived threats on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. When you moved about the city, you being a UN employee, did you wear UN insignia to designate your neutrality?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My helmet was blue. We wore blue vests, we had white vehicles with UN markings and UN flags. The vehicles -- can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military observers' point of view, all the vehicles we used were soft-skinned vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you feel any degree of safety moving around the civilian areas, and can you comment on the comparative degree of safety between moving around the civilian areas and the front line?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make a distinction would be foolish if one considered that one was going to be safer in one rather than the other. The whole city was an extremely dangerous place to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At any stage did you make any assessment of the numbers of civilian casualties on the Bosnian government side which were unrelated to military activity?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at our reports that we received from both the Presidency side, from our own observations as we drove around the city, we worked out an average of about 14 or 15 people dying per day, but that's only an average, and I think the numbers numerically over the whole siege of Sarajevo would probably work out to about 14 or 15 a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said you had access to the Bosnian government figures. Did you mitigate them in any way? In other words, did you accept them at face value or did you factor in a degree of exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I considered that our observation capability was sometimes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. better in terms of determining the numbers that I've just given you, of our own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to move on to a new topic. Would that be a convenient place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, because we, of course, have to reschedule this day as well. We started at 8.30. We'll have a break now until 10.30. We'll then continue until 12.00, and we'll have a break from -- until 12.20, and then we'll continue until a quarter to 2.00. We'll have a break now until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just grant me one second. As I indicated before, it is difficult for the Chamber to come to final conclusions in respect of the submissions made by the Prosecution. Nevertheless, the Prosecution asked some guidance, especially in view of the coming week. I'll give at least some guidance. The Chamber will be more strict in keeping the time limits for the Defence that they will not use more time for cross-examination as used for examination-in-chief. Of course, there always might be exceptions, such as if the Prosecution would indicate that they would use two hours and they just use half an hour, then that would not automatically mean that we would then, after 30 minutes, say to the Defence that their time is over. So it always depends, but we will be far more strict that the time used for cross-examination will not be more than the examination-in-chief. The second issue is that we spend a lot of time on procedural issues. If they are directly related to the testimony given at that moment, the admission of documents or objections and questions, of course we have to hear them immediately, but we'll not at an average spend more than 15 minutes a day on general procedural issues. And we'll try to do that also as efficiently as possible. That might mean that we try to gain time in, for example, starting earlier or just using the last ten minutes of the day for these kind of procedural issues. The Chamber is very much concerned about the Prosecution's case not being finished before the summer recess. Keeping in mind what I've just said, and also keeping in mind that, at an average, the Chamber intends to grant approximately 50 per cent of the time asked by the Defence to cross-examine expert witnesses, the Chamber would highly appreciate if the Prosecution would use the next week to reconsider the time schedule as it has been presented by now and to see whether a time schedule could be created such that the Prosecution's case would be concluded not later than the beginning of the summer recess. This is the guidance we could give after just a brief period of deliberation. Apart from that, you asked some guidance as far as the application for granting a certificate in respect of Witness AD is concerned. A written decision will be delivered, but the decision will be that the certificate will not be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I may finally indicate, where I just said that we would be very strict on the time to be used in cross-examination, of course there's a direct relation between the time used in examination-in-chief. We sometimes saw that the Prosecution was able to use far less time, but sometimes we also had to experience that the Prosecution took more time, sometimes dealing very extensively with issues, very specific issues, of which it is not, at first sight, clear whether they would justify such a lot of time. So therefore, we'll also be rather strict, and we know that time gained by the Prosecution usually is double gain. It will affect, in general, the time used in cross-examination as well. It's to both parties to use that time as efficiently as possible. Having given this guidance, I think we could continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Mole. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I'm informed that it might be that at a later stage this morning your examination might be interrupted again, which is a very unhappy -- an un -- it's not the preferable way of doing it, but sometimes there might be no alternative. I again hope you'll understand. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit D131, which was formerly tendered this morning in relation to the evidence of Witness W. I don't think that's a confidential exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think everything is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Perhaps we should then go into closed session for this part of the examination-in-chief. It won't be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into closed session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the visits that you made, I think you said two or three times a week, to the Lima observation posts, did you ever personally observe any instances of what you believed to be the indiscriminate fire of the city with heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will appreciate that when you're on a gun site and weapons fire, you are not party to the range map which the commander is using to determine his target. As a result, I always asked that my UN military observers - and therefore I as well - would ask local commanders what their target was, in an attempt to determine whether it was acceptable as a target or not. We were, by virtue of the system I've described, only as effective as the answer that I was given by the local commander, but that did not prevent us persisting in the attempt to reduce the level of tension created upon the city by reducing the numbers of rounds fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, are you saying that you would instruct your subordinates to bring pressure to bear on the local commanders when they were concerned about the firing by persistently questioning them as to the nature of the target? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever do that personally?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did you ever receive answers that you regarded as unsatisfactory?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received answers from the trivial, such as the commander telling me, when firing his mortar rounds, that he was warming the barrels. Albeit I accept warming the barrels is a requirement if you have a fire mission and you then proceed with that fire mission, but the instances that I recall, the firing ceased after a few rounds, whether for my intervention or not, I can't determine, but it rather negated the original reason for firing the weapons in the first instance, to warm the barrels before proceeding on a fire mission. That was one example. On other occasions, one particular one, I was told that the three rounds that had been fired were one for each finger of the Serb salute. I don't consider either of those reasons to be pertinent, reasonable, tactical, or strategic reasons for firing one's weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the incident where you were given the -- incident or incidents where you were given the explanation of warming the barrels, were you able to draw any conclusions as to where the round or rounds were likely to land?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rationale for firing the weapon that had been given to me was as irrational and as vague as the assumed target; in other words, I don't think there was a specific target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you able to form any view as to whether the rounds fired on that occasion threatened, potentially, civilians?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that the rounds were random, in that they were fired towards the city of Sarajevo, there's a very high percentage chance that they were random and fired into civilian areas, because it was not explained to me that they were targeting a military target. I've told you the reasons why they fired the weapons. That would hardly be a sensible answer if they had a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the weapon, or what were the weapons involved, first in the incident -- I think you told us that was a mortar?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the Serb salute, what was the weapon or the weapons involved?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were artillery weapons. I can't remember their nomenclature, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And whereabouts were they pointed at the time of firing, those artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the weapons around Sarajevo commanded by the Romanija Corps were pointing towards the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever complain to General Galic about those incidents, and similar incidents, of indiscriminate fire, as observed by you and your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most days when we did meet, clearly the topic of discussion was the siege of Sarajevo and indiscriminate fire or intense fire was mentioned, as was pertinent at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you saying, in effect, that as a matter of routine you would do that, you would complain of indiscriminate fire, as observed by yourself and your subordinates to him?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I add that the rider that you'll recall I talked about the persistent background of fire coming into the city daily. I wouldn't trivialise that, but what I am saying is that we concentrated on the peaks of that incoming fire more than we did on what we perceived as the norm. I hope I've explained myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying to us that the level of fire into Sarajevo was such that you effectively had to adjust your standard of normalcy; and secondly, that adjustment was of necessity reflected in the frequency and nature of your complaints to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly the case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And again, I'm seeking only to reflect your evidence, and please tell me if I'm correctly stating it.

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You say it better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But the end result of that was that many incidents that one would normally complain of, because of the exigencies of the situation, went without complaint and you had to focus on the more serious incidents?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the correct interpretation, and that is the reason why I persist with trying to explain this constant background of incoming fire. It was taken as a norm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that you made these regular complaints. Can you tell us what his response was to these complaints?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can probably do that to the best effect if I give an example of a particular meeting. I believe it was in November 1992, where I hadn't been able to get across to Lukavica for about a week and a half. It might have been two weeks. And when we initially met, General Galic suggested that I hadn't been to see him for a while, and my immediate reaction was one of considerable anger, because the reason I hadn't been able to go across the airport was that the intensity of shelling was such that I had placed a restriction of movement on all UN military observers, including myself. So clearly, once I had expressed the reason why I hadn't been able to come across and meet him, I naturally asked what the objective was. This would not be an unusual question in our meetings. I never recall getting what I would consider a tactical or strategic answer, in military terms, to that question. The conversation tended to be tangential to that issue and be removed to other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On occasions when he did offer -- well, first of all, were there occasions when he did offer some sort of explanation?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There would be the constant response that the Muslims, that being his expression, not mine, were attacking in a particular sector of the city, which of course, with the observation points that we had, both within and outside the city, we were in a position to verify, or otherwise, and I don't ever recall the local tactical situation changing to the degree that would realistically permit the response of weaponry being fired into the city as an appropriate military response.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Well, on those occasions when he sought to justify the fire into the city on the basis that it was in response to using his words, as you've related it, as a result of a Muslim attack in a particular sector, did you ever say to him, given your explanation, that your subordinates were able to confirm that in fact there was no offensive by the Bosnian government forces?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the example I gave you, to best serve to answer the question: Because I was unable to cross the airport for such a period of time, we had that time to analyse what was militarily happening within the city. So I was informed before the meeting that nothing of significance was occurring, and hence the reason for my questioning of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was his response then?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much the same as I've described before, leading onto other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you met with General Galic, in what language did you and he communicate?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke in English, he spoke in his own language, and the translator did the business between us. That was our translator, the UN-employed translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At any of those meetings did he have a translator or interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall one as such. My preference, obviously, would be to take my own interpreter. How much Captain Indzic knew of English and interpreted, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean to imply by that comment that Captain Indzic was present?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we said earlier this week, he was present at a number of the meetings, understandable to a degree that one should have somebody else to make sure that interpretation was correct. So understanding that viewpoint caused me not to be concerned about his presence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever have any concerns as to the ability of your UN-employed interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you always use the same interpreter or different interpreters?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I always used the one that was directly employed by the UN on Lukavica side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, are you saying that the UN had an interpreter permanently positioned at Lukavica for the assistance of UN staff?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did General Galic ever say to you words which you regarded as conveying an intention to shell the city indiscriminately?

utterances.speaker: Richard Mole [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my original witness statement given in 1997 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I would like to object to this question because we see that we have the presence of an interpreter, which is necessary, and we have to underline that if words were uttered, they could only have been uttered through the channel of the interpreter, and I think you should rephrase your question in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, when asked what General Galic ever said, the Chamber takes it that you were asked what General Galic would have said as far as it was interpreted to you by an interpreter. Please proceed. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is somebody expecting me to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll repeat the question to you.
